body:
Formation of a solar eclipse

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks part or all of the Sun's visible disc for observers in certain regions of Earth.

The required order of alignment is Sun, Moon and Earth. A solar eclipse can therefore occur only during the new moon phase.

Although the Sun is much larger than the Moon, it is also much farther from Earth. Their apparent angular sizes in Earth's sky are consequently similar, making it possible for the Moon to cover the entire visible solar disc under suitable conditions.

The three regions of the Moon's shadow

Because the Sun is an extended source of light rather than a single point, the Moon's shadow has regions with different degrees of solar obstruction.

  • Umbra: The central shadow region in which the Moon completely blocks the visible disc of the Sun.
  • Penumbra: The outer shadow region in which the Moon blocks only part of the visible solar disc.
  • Antumbra: The region beyond the tip of the umbra, where the Moon appears completely inside the larger solar disc without covering its outer edge.

Types of solar eclipses

Total solar eclipse

A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon's apparent disc is large enough to cover the entire visible disc of the Sun and its umbra reaches Earth's surface.

Observers located within the narrow path of the umbra experience totality. During totality, daylight becomes substantially darker and the Sun's outer atmosphere, known as the corona, may become visible.

Partial solar eclipse

A partial solar eclipse occurs when the Moon covers only a portion of the solar disc as seen by an observer. The observer is within the Moon's penumbra.

Observers outside the central path of a total or annular eclipse may also experience a partial eclipse.

Annular solar eclipse

An annular solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes centrally across the Sun but its apparent diameter is smaller than that of the Sun.

The Moon therefore fails to cover the entire solar disc. A bright ring of sunlight remains visible around its dark silhouette. This appearance is popularly known as the ring of fire.

Annularity occurs within the Moon's antumbra. It is more likely when the Moon is relatively far from Earth, towards its apogee, and consequently appears smaller in the sky. The apparent size of the Sun also influences whether a central eclipse is total or annular.

Hybrid solar eclipse

A hybrid solar eclipse appears total along some portions of its central path and annular along other portions. This can occur because the curvature of Earth's surface changes the distance between observers and the Moon along the eclipse path.

Geographical visibility

A solar eclipse is visible only from regions of Earth reached by the Moon's shadow and experiencing daylight at that time.

The central path of a total or annular eclipse is relatively narrow, while a partial eclipse can be visible over a considerably wider geographical area.

Totality at a particular location usually lasts only a few minutes, although the complete passage through the partial and central phases may last much longer.

Safe observation

Direct observation of the bright solar disc requires appropriate solar eclipse glasses or other properly designed solar-viewing protection. Ordinary sunglasses are not sufficient.

During a total solar eclipse, direct viewing without solar filters is safe only during confirmed complete totality. Protection must be used again as soon as any part of the bright solar disc reappears.

Partial and annular solar eclipses have no safe unprotected direct-viewing phase. Indirect observation using a pinhole projector is another safe method.

Prelims focus

  • Solar eclipse alignment: Sun, Moon, Earth.
  • A solar eclipse can occur only at new moon.
  • Total eclipse: umbra.
  • Partial eclipse: penumbra.
  • Annular eclipse: antumbra and ring of fire.
  • Trap: An annular eclipse is not a total eclipse and cannot be viewed directly without appropriate solar protection.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 17, p. 227; NCERT, Class 6, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 11, Light, Shadows and Reflections, pp. 110-111; NASA, Types of Solar Eclipses and Eclipse Viewing Safety, consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Formation of a lunar eclipse

A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, causing the Moon to move through Earth's shadow.

The required order of alignment is Sun, Earth and Moon. A lunar eclipse can therefore occur only during a full moon.

Unlike a solar eclipse, in which the Moon blocks the Sun from an observer's view, a lunar eclipse occurs because Earth obstructs the sunlight that would otherwise directly illuminate the Moon.

Types of lunar eclipses

Total lunar eclipse

A total lunar eclipse occurs when the entire visible disc of the Moon enters Earth's umbra, the central region of Earth's shadow where direct sunlight is blocked.

During totality, the Moon does not necessarily disappear. It often remains visible with a reddish or copper-coloured appearance.

Partial lunar eclipse

A partial lunar eclipse occurs when only a portion of the Moon enters Earth's umbra. The portion within the umbra appears distinctly darker than the rest of the lunar disc.

Penumbral lunar eclipse

A penumbral lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes through Earth's penumbra without entering its umbra. Only part of the incoming sunlight is obstructed in this region.

The Moon becomes slightly dimmer, and the change in brightness may be difficult to notice with the unaided eye.

Why the Moon appears red during a total lunar eclipse

During a total lunar eclipse, Earth blocks direct sunlight from reaching the Moon. However, some sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, bends into the shadow region and reaches the lunar surface.

As sunlight travels through the atmosphere, shorter wavelengths, particularly blue and violet light, are scattered more strongly. Longer wavelengths, particularly red and orange light, are transmitted more effectively through this long atmospheric path.

The transmitted and refracted sunlight gives the eclipsed Moon its characteristic reddish appearance. A totally eclipsed Moon with this appearance is popularly called a blood moon.

The precise colour and brightness vary depending on atmospheric conditions, including the presence of dust, aerosols and clouds.

Visibility and duration

A lunar eclipse can be observed from locations on Earth's nighttime side where the Moon is above the horizon. Consequently, it is generally visible across a much larger geographical region than a total solar eclipse.

A lunar eclipse may last several hours because the Moon takes considerable time to pass through Earth's extensive shadow.

All stages of a lunar eclipse are safe to observe with the unaided eye. Special solar-viewing filters are not required.

Comparison of solar and lunar eclipses

FeatureSolar eclipseLunar eclipse
AlignmentSun, Moon, EarthSun, Earth, Moon
Lunar phaseNew moonFull moon
Shadow-producing bodyMoonEarth
Observed duringDaytimeNighttime
VisibilityRestricted geographical regionMuch of the nighttime hemisphere
Principal typesTotal, partial, annular, hybridTotal, partial, penumbral
Direct viewingSolar protection required except during complete totalitySafe without special protection

Distinguishing the principal astronomical phenomena

Earth's daily rotation produces day and night. Its annual revolution combined with axial tilt produces seasons, solstices and equinoxes. Its changing distance from the Sun produces the orbital positions called perihelion and aphelion.

Solar and lunar eclipses are different phenomena. They require a suitable alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon near the nodes of the Moon's inclined orbit.

Thus, daily illumination, seasonal changes, orbital distances and eclipses are related to celestial motions but must be explained using their respective physical causes.

Prelims focus

  • Lunar eclipse alignment: Sun, Earth, Moon.
  • A lunar eclipse can occur only at full moon.
  • Total lunar eclipse: the entire Moon enters Earth's umbra.
  • A penumbral lunar eclipse does not involve entry into Earth's umbra.
  • The reddish appearance of a totally eclipsed Moon results from sunlight passing through Earth's atmosphere.
  • Trap: An annular eclipse is a type of solar eclipse, not a type of lunar eclipse.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 17, p. 227; NASA, Eclipses and the Moon, sections on Lunar Eclipse Basics, Types of Lunar Eclipses and Blood Moon; NASA, Eclipses and Eclipse Viewing Safety; NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapter 3, pp. 18-21; online references consulted 26 November 2026.]
